screens.title: Performance Monitoring & Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Performance monitoring is the practice of watching C P U, memory, disk input and output and network input and output so you can spot bottlenecks before they affect users. In this chapter we treat these four resources as lanes or pipes: when one lane fills, traffic backs up and the system slows. You will learn practical commands that give real-time and historical views, how to interpret load averages and swap activity, and a repeatable troubleshooting workflow to identify the root cause. We’ll also show how to find and handle runaway processes and how simple limits like ulimit can prevent a single user or process from taking down a server. By the end you’ll be able to collect evidence, choose the right tool, and decide whether to tune, restart, or add capacity. Think of this as a detective process: gather facts, isolate the lane that is saturated, and act on the smallest reliable change that improves response time.

screens.title: CPU Monitoring with top, htop, and mpstat
screens.narratorSegment: C P U monitoring begins with a simple claim: if the C P U lane is saturated, processes wait for execution time and responsiveness drops. The interactive tools top and htop show real-time per-process C P U percent and load averages. Load averages are a compact signal: they show the average number of runnable or uninterruptible processes over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. A useful rule is to compare load averages to the number of C P U cores; a load much higher than core count indicates C P U contention. Use mpstat -P ALL to inspect each core. This detects cases where one core is maxed while others sit idle; that pattern often points to a single-threaded process or improper C P U affinity. A concrete example: run top, observe a process showing 95% C P U on one core while the 1-minute load is near the core count. Run mpstat -P ALL 1 and watch the per-core usage spike on a single C P U. A common misconception is assuming high C P U always means you need more cores; instead first inspect what the offending process is doing and whether it can be optimized or restarted. Key actions: identify the PID in top or htop, inspect its logs or command line, and test terminating a runaway process carefully. Takeaway: collect both per-process and per-core metrics before deciding to add capacity.

content.html:
Core Concept › CPU Monitoring
Commands & Example
Run these commands to observe CPU behavior in real time and per-core detail.
top
htop    # If installed, provides color and navigation
mpstat -P ALL 1    # per-core CPU stats every 1 second
Example
You see load average 12.00 on a 4-core host and a process at 95% CPU. Use mpstat to confirm only one core is saturated.
Common mistake
Assuming high CPU means add CPUs. Often a bad query or tight loop should be fixed first.
Interpretation bullets
  • Load average > core count suggests CPU contention. Confirm with per-core usage.
  • High %us indicates user-space CPU time; high %wa indicates processes waiting on I/O, not CPU.
  • mpstat shows whether one core is overloaded; that points to single-threaded bottlenecks.
Key Takeaway

Use both per-process and per-core views. Diagnose the cause before adding hardware.

screens.title: Memory Monitoring: free and vmstat
screens.narratorSegment: Memory pressure is a frequent and subtle cause of slow systems. A key point is that Linux uses spare R A M for cache and buffers, so the raw 'free' column is a poor indicator of health. Instead focus on the 'available' field in free -h; it estimates memory that can be used without swapping. Use vmstat to see short-term trends and swap activity: the si and so columns report swap in and swap out. High values in si/so indicate the kernel is moving pages to or from disk, which is slow and causes latency. A concrete example: run free -h and find available memory under 200MB with swap nearly full; then run vmstat 1 and see repeated non-zero si/so — this is classic memory exhaustion. A common misconception is to immediately add swap; swap can mask the problem but will slow applications. Prefer finding the process that holds large memory, resizing or restarting it, or adding physical R A M when the working set truly exceeds available memory. Practice: use free -h, then vmstat 1 5, and inspect processes in top sorted by memory. Ask yourself which process holds the largest resident set and whether it can be tuned or restarted.

content.html:
Definition › Memory Monitoring
Commands
Use these to examine current memory and short-term swapping.
free -h
vmstat 1 5  # report every 1 second for 5 samples
# In vmstat, watch 'si' and 'so' columns for swap activity
Example
Available memory at 200M and swap nearly full; vmstat shows si and so > 0 — system is swapping and will be slow.
Interpretation bullets
  • Free -h: trust the 'available' field, not raw 'free'.
  • vmstat: si/so show swap in/out activity; sustained values mean active swapping.
  • When swapping is high, identify large-resident processes in top and consider restarting or tuning them.
Misconception

Adding swap is not always the right fix. It can hide memory pressure while users suffer from slow disk-backed paging.

Key Takeaway

Use available memory and vmstat’s si/so to decide whether to tune apps, restart processes, or add RAM.

screens.title: Disk I/O Monitoring with iostat and df
screens.narratorSegment: Disk input and output problems often translate directly into slow application response, especially for databases and storage-heavy workloads. The iostat tool reports reads, writes, device utilization and latency. Key metrics are %util, r/s and w/s, kilobytes per second, and await. A high %util near 100 percent means the device was busy and likely a bottleneck. High await indicates long input and output service times. Use iostat -xz 1 to get extended per-device stats. Also check df -h for disk fill levels; a full filesystem can cause surprising failures even if IO rates are modest. A concrete example: run iostat -xz 1 while issuing a large write with dd to simulate load. You will see %util climb and await rise. A common mistake is viewing only throughput without latency; throughput can be high while await is also high, indicating slow response. Practical steps: identify the device (sda, nvme0n1), check %util and await, inspect filesystem usage with df -h, and consider IO scheduler, asynchronous tasks, or moving data to faster storage. Key takeaway: latency matters as much as megabytes per second. Disk I/O Monitoring with iostat and df means watch both %util and await. high utilization with high await points to a slow device, not just heavy throughput.. In practical terms, interpret %util, await, throughput and spot full disks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow › Disk I/O Monitoring
Commands to run
Collect per-device I/O stats and check disk usage.
iostat -xz 1    # extended stats, per device, every 1 second
df -h            # check disk capacity and used space
# Simulate disk load:
# dd if=/dev/zero of=largefile bs=1M count=1000 conv=fdatasync
Scenario
Running dd to write a 1GB file should raise %util and await on the device where the file lives.
Interpretation bullets
  • %util near 100% means device was busy; consider faster storage or spreading load.
  • r/s and w/s show operations per second; rkB/s and wkB/s show throughput in KB/s.
  • High await signals slow I/O response time even if throughput looks acceptable.
Common mistake

Focusing only on throughput numbers without checking await and %util can miss true latency problems.

Key Takeaway

When I/O latency rises, applications often slow more than throughput measures suggest. Use iostat and df together.

screens.title: Network I/O: sar and real-time tools
screens.narratorSegment: Network saturation can mimic other bottlenecks. The sar utility with the DEV option reports per-interface rx and tx rates and helps you see trends over time. Use sar -n DEV 1 to sample traffic every second. Key counters include rxkB/s and txkB/s. For real-time per-connection views try iftop or nload to see which flows consume bandwidth. A concrete example: run sar -n DEV 1 and notice rxkB/s rising close to the interface capacity during a backup; iftop will show the IP addresses responsible. A common misconception is to assume all high network rates are problematic — if your link is provisioned for that throughput and latency remains low, high utilization may be normal. Instead look for saturation that causes packet drops or increased latency. Practical steps: identify which interface is busy, check link speed and errors with ethtool, inspect rx/tx rates with sar or iftop, and consider rate-limiting or moving large transfers to off-peak windows. Always correlate network metrics with application response times so you act on real bottlenecks, not expected traffic spikes. Network I/O: sar and real-time tools means use sar for historical interface rates and iftop for per-connection views; correlate traffic with latency and packet errors before acting.. In practical terms, detect saturated interfaces and per-connection bandwidth use. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison › Network I/O
Commands
Collect interface-level and flow-level metrics.
sar -n DEV 1        # interface rx/tx rates every 1 second
iftop               # interactive per-connection bandwidth view
nload               # simple real-time bandwidth per interface
Example
During a backup you may see rxkB/s near link speed. iftop reveals the backup host as the top talker.
Interpretation bullets
  • Watch rxkB/s and txkB/s for sustained saturation; correlate with packet drops or RTT increases.
  • Use iftop to find which peers or ports dominate bandwidth; that helps target rate limits.
  • High utilization alone is not always bad; check latency and errors to decide.
Misconception

Assuming high bandwidth usage equals a fault. If latency is low and link is expected to be busy, no remediation may be needed.

Key Takeaway

Combine historical sar data with real-time iftop views and latency checks to decide if the network is the bottleneck.

screens.title: Identifying Runaway Processes, ulimit, and Troubleshooting Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: When a single process consumes excessive resources it can bring the whole system down. The workflow in the chapter gives a clear sequence: start with top or htop to get a quick system view; identify whether C P U, memory, disk, or network is the likely bottleneck; then drill down with the specialized tool for that resource. For runaway processes, locate the PID and check its command line, open files, and logs. Use kill or restart the service as appropriate; kill -9 should be a last resort because it prevents graceful cleanup. To prevent recurrence, set resource limits with ulimit or via system configuration files such as /etc/security/limits. conf; for example limiting open files per group reduces the risk of descriptor exhaustion. A concrete example: discover multiple bash loops spawned in the background with top, confirm with ps aux | grep bash, then kill the offending PIDs and add a ulimit entry for the user group to cap nofile. Common mistakes include jumping to hardware upgrades before investigating the faulty process and misinterpreting cached memory as free. Close investigations by verifying performance after the change and by collecting historical data with sar to confirm the issue is resolved. Question for reflection: after stopping a runaway process, what evidence will you collect to prevent it from recurring?

content.html:
Process Flow › Runaway Processes & Workflow
Troubleshooting Steps
  1. Start with top or htop to get a quick view of CPU and memory usage.
  2. Identify the likely bottleneck: CPU load, low available memory, high %util, or saturated rx/tx.
  3. Drill down with the specific tool: vmstat, mpstat, iostat, or sar.
  4. Locate the offending PID, inspect logs, and decide whether to restart or kill the process.
  5. Implement preventive limits with ulimit or limits.conf to avoid future resource exhaustion.
# Example commands used in this flow
top
ps aux | grep 
kill 
# Example ulimit limit in /etc/security/limits.conf
# @webusers hard nofile 1024
Supporting cards
Concrete example
You find a background loop consuming CPU: run ps to find PIDs, kill them, then add a nofile or nproc limit for that user group.
Pro tip
Collect a short sar history before and after remediation to prove the fix and inform future capacity planning.
Common mistake
Using kill -9 immediately. Prefer graceful termination and confirm service behavior in logs first.
Key Takeaway

Use a repeatable observe→identify→drill→resolve workflow, and enforce limits so one process cannot exhaust shared resources.

screens.title: Install and enable monitoring tools
screens.narratorSegment: Before you can diagnose intermittent performance issues, you need a reproducible way to collect both real-time and historical data. Install the lightweight packages sysstat and htop on your system. htop gives a colored, interactive view of processes and per-core usage for quick triage. sysstat provides the sar, iostat, and mpstat commands that record system activity to disk so you can analyze trends after the fact. On Debian or Ubuntu use the package manager to install and on RHEL derivatives use dnf or yum. After installation, enable or configure the service that records sar data; many distributions require enabling and starting the sysstat service so daily binary logs are written to slash var slash log slash sa. A concrete example: install, enable the service, and verify that slash var slash log slash sa contains files. A common misconception is that sar runs automatically right after package install; often you need to enable collection or adjust cron/systemd timers. Finally, confirm htop launches and sar -V reports a version. This preparation ensures you can gather live snapshots with htop and long-term trends with sar, which together let you spot momentary spikes versus sustained degradation. What small test will you run to confirm data is being recorded?

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Install & Enable Tools

Install and enable monitoring tools

Get sysstat and htop installed, start sar collection, and verify logs for later analysis.

Definition
Commands to install and enable
Example package commands and service enable steps for common distros.
# Debian/Ubuntu
sudo apt update && sudo apt install sysstat htop -y
sudo systemctl enable --now sysstat

# RHEL/CentOS/Fedora
sudo dnf install sysstat htop -y
sudo systemctl enable --now sysstat

# Verify sar logs
ls -l /var/log/sa
sar -V
Quick verification checks
  • Run htop and confirm per-core bars and processes appear.
  • Check for sar data files in /var/log/sa or use sar -f.
  • Ensure a systemd timer or cron is active so sar collects periodically.
Key Takeaway

Install both live and historical tools; live tools give instant context, sar gives the trend history you need to diagnose intermittent problems.

Notes & common pitfalls
Things admins often miss when enabling historical collection.

Many assume sar starts immediately after install. Confirm by listing /var/log/sa. If files are missing, check the sysstat configuration or enable the timer. Also ensure log rotation won't remove the short-term history you need for troubleshooting.

Coming up
Enable collection
Verify logs
Run htop
Check /var/log/sa
Example: enable and test
# enable and start sysstat
sudo systemctl enable --now sysstat
# wait a minute, then show recent sar output
sar -u 1 3

screens.title: Generate safe CPU and disk loads
screens.narratorSegment: When diagnosing performance, controlled reproductions are invaluable. You can gently stress C P U and disk to observe how the system responds and which metrics change. For C P U testing, a tight background loop is an easy tool: run an innocuous busy loop in a new shell to raise C P U usage and watch htop and the load averages rise. For disk input and output, a buffered write like the dd command copying from slash dev slash zero to a large file simulates sustained write traffic; monitor iostat -xz 1 to watch %util, r slash s and await change. Always test on non-production systems or use limited counts and smaller file sizes: the common mistake is running an unlimited test that floods production disks or fills capacity. A concrete example is to run one short C P U worker per core and a dd that writes 1 gigabyte — observe htop, iostat and sar simultaneously. Interpret results: high load average with low disk %util points to C P U contention; near 100% device %util and rising await indicate a disk bottleneck. After the test, clean up temporary files and stop background loops. This controlled approach gives clear cause-and-effect between the workload you created and the metrics recorded, and it teaches you how to read the changes in real time and from sar logs later.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Create Load Safely

Generate safe CPU and disk loads

Use bounded loops and dd with limited counts to simulate stress without harming production.

Process
CPU load example
Run a limited background loop to stress CPU cores safely.
# Spawn one CPU worker in background (stop with kill)
while true; do :; done &
# Repeat per core if testing multi-core behaviour

# After testing, find and kill the background loops
ps -u $USER -o pid,cmd | grep "while true" | awk '{print $1}' | xargs -r kill
Disk I/O example
Use dd with a bounded size to avoid filling disks; watch iostat for `%util` and `await`.
# write 1GB file and sync to measure throughput
dd if=/dev/zero of=./largefile bs=1M count=1024 conv=fdatasync
# monitor device activity
iostat -xz 1
Common Mistake

Running unbounded tests or very large dd operations on production storage can cause outages. Always constrain test size and time.

What you should observe
  • CPU test: per-core %CPU rises; load average increases; context switches may increase.
  • Disk test: `%util` approaches device saturation, `await` increases, throughput columns show rkB/wkB changes.
  • Use sar to confirm changes persisted beyond the immediate window.
Example observation snippet
# iostat snippet during dd
Device:         r/s     w/s   rkB/s  wkB/s  await  %util
sda             0.0   500.0     0  51200  20.1   98.7

# Interpretation: device nearly saturated, high await indicates slow response
Why this matters

Controlled tests create reproducible evidence you can use to decide whether to optimize the application, change configuration, or provision faster hardware.

screens.title: Use sar to analyze historical trends
screens.narratorSegment: Performance issues are often intermittent: they happen at peak hours or during irregular jobs. That's where sar becomes indispensable. sar reads binary data files generated by sysstat and summarizes C P U, memory, input and output, and network activity over time. Start by identifying available sar files in slash var slash log slash sa and use sar -u -f to show historical C P U usage or sar -n DEV -f for network interfaces. Look at the timestamps and compare busy windows to expected workload schedules. A concrete example: if users report slow response at 02:00, open the sar file for that day and run sar -u -f slash var slash log slash sa slash sa21 to inspect C P U averages around that time. Remember to compare sar reports across days to rule out one-off spikes. A common misconception is treating a single high reading as evidence of a persistent problem. Instead, analyze the pattern: isolated spikes require different remediation than sustained high usage. Use sar's per-interval output to correlate events — for example, a cron job that runs hourly may align with disk await increases. Finally, export sar data to CSV if you need to plot trends externally. Historical analysis lets you move from guesswork to evidence-based decisions about tuning or capacity planning.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Historical sar Analysis

Use sar to analyze historical trends

Read daily sar logs to correlate slowdowns with scheduled events and recurring spikes.

Timeline
Common sar commands
Examples to inspect historical CPU, device, and network metrics.
# Show CPU history from a specific sa file
sar -u -f /var/log/sa/sa21

# Show network device stats
sar -n DEV -f /var/log/sa/sa21

# show device IO history
iostat -x -f /var/log/sa/sa21  # iostat reads current devices; use sar for history
How to read sar output
  • Match timestamps to the reported intervals to find busy windows.
  • Look for repeated high `%usr` or `%system` for CPU issues and high `await` or `%util` for disks.
  • Correlate sar spikes with cron jobs, backups, or batch windows.
Pro Tip

Keep at least several days of sar data to detect periodic patterns. If logs are rotated too frequently, adjust retention in sysstat config.

Example scenario

Users report slow responses nightly around 02:00. Inspect `sa` files for the last week at 02:00. If disk `await` spikes every night, you likely have a scheduled backup or log rotate overlapping heavy IO.

# inspect 02:00 interval across several days (pseudo-steps)
for f in /var/log/sa/sa2[0-7]; do sar -u -f "$f" | grep "02:00"; done
Misconception check

Don't treat a single spike as a system-wide issue. Instead, ask: does this repeat? If not, find what ran at that exact time before escalating to hardware changes.

Next step

If a pattern is found, drill down to the process using `ps`, check logs, and adjust schedules or resource allocation accordingly.

screens.title: Set ulimit and persistent resource limits
screens.narratorSegment: Preventing a single user or process from exhausting system resources is an important defensive step. ulimit controls shell-level resource limits like the number of open files, maximum memory size, and number of processes. Use ulimit -n to view or set the open file limit for the current shell; changes here are immediate but ephemeral. For persistent, system-wide or user-specific limits, configure slash etc slash security slash limits. conf or drop files into slash etc slash security slash limits. d. For example, to limit members of a webusers group to 1024 open files, add a line that sets hard nofile 1024 for @webusers. A common pitfall is to assume limits. conf applies to services started by systemd. To enforce limits for systemd-managed services, set Limit NOFILE equals or other Limit directives directly in the unit file, because systemd does not always read PAM limits for services. A concrete example: update limits. conf, relogin to a shell, then verify ulimit -n reflects the new limit. Also, test failure modes by creating a process that hits the limit; a graceful failure is preferable to a system-wide crash. In short, ulimit provides immediate control, limits. conf makes those controls persistent for interactive logins, and systemd unit directives are necessary for services started at boot. Which limit will you set first to protect critical services?

keyIdea.text: Apply ulimits and persistent limits to avoid a single user or daemon from consuming all file descriptors, processes, or memory.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › ulimit & limits.conf

Set ulimit and persistent resource limits

Use shell limits for quick tests and limits.conf or systemd directives for persistent policies.

Definition
Quick commands
Use these to inspect and set limits interactively or persistently.
# show current open file limit
ulimit -n
# set soft limit in current shell
ulimit -Sn 1024
# set hard limit in current shell
ulimit -Hn 2048

# /etc/security/limits.conf (example)
# @webusers hard nofile 1024
# @webusers soft nofile 512
Systemd note
Services may ignore PAM limits. Use unit directives to enforce limits for daemons.
# example /etc/systemd/system/your.service.d/limits.conf
[Service]
LimitNOFILE=1024

# then reload and restart
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart your.service
Common Mistake

Setting only shell limits without updating systemd units leaves services unprotected when they start at boot.

How to test after changes
  • Log out and back in to apply limits.conf for interactive sessions, then run ulimit -n.
  • For services, set Limit directives and restart the unit to verify with systemctl show.
  • Simulate resource exhaustion with a safe test to confirm graceful failure modes.
Analogy

Think of ulimits as per-user faucets. Without a regulator, one faucet can flood the house. Limits keep each faucet within safe capacity.

Practical step

Decide on critical services and set explicit limits in their systemd units, then add broader user limits via limits.conf.

screens.title: A disciplined troubleshooting checklist
screens.narratorSegment: A consistent workflow turns guesswork into reliable troubleshooting. Start with a snapshot: run top or htop for a high-level view of C P U, memory, and processes. Next, identify which resource shows abnormal signals: high load averages, low available memory, high disk %util, or saturated network interfaces. Then drill down using specialized tools: vmstat for memory and swap activity, iostat for device delays and sar for historical corroboration. Identify the culprit process with ps or by filtering top, and examine its logs and configuration. Decide whether to restart or gracefully stop the service; use kill only when necessary and prefer SIGTERM before SIGKILL. After remediation, monitor to confirm the problem is resolved and that no secondary issues appear. Include these additional checks in your routine: check for full disks with df -h, ensure ulimits are adequate, and review scheduled tasks that might coincide with the spike. A common mistake is assuming that adding C P U or R A M fixes the problem; optimization or configuration changes can be cheaper and faster. Finish by documenting findings and any changes you made so you can spot recurring patterns next time. This disciplined loop — observe, identify, drill down, remediate, and confirm — reduces risk and speeds recovery. Which step in the flow would you automate in your environment?

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Troubleshooting Checklist

A disciplined troubleshooting checklist

A repeatable flow avoids missteps and leads to reliable fixes.

Process Flow
Checklist (numbered)
  1. Snapshot with `htop`/`top` to see CPU, memory, and top processes.
  2. Identify the bottleneck resource: CPU, memory, disk I/O, or network.
  3. Use focused tools: `vmstat`, `iostat`, `mpstat`, `sar`, `ss`/`sar -n DEV`.
  4. Find the process and inspect logs, configs, and recent deployments.
  5. Mitigate: restart service gracefully, tune configs, or kill a runaway process if needed.
  6. Confirm resolution with continued monitoring and update documentation.
Commands to validate each step
# snapshot
htop
# memory and swap patterns
vmstat 1 5
# disk device wait and util
iostat -xz 1 3
# historical check
sar -u -f /var/log/sa/sa21
# check listening sockets and connections
ss -tuln
Key Takeaway

A repeatable checklist speeds diagnosis and avoids knee-jerk fixes. Always confirm the fix and document the root cause.

Example remediation steps
  • If high CPU from a process: investigate logs, limit or restart it, consider query or code optimization.
  • If heavy swap: add RAM, tune caching, or reduce memory footprint; avoid relying on swap for performance.
  • If disk `%util` is 100%: move I/O-heavy work, use faster storage, or stagger heavy jobs.
Documentation & post-mortem

Record what you observed, the actions you took, and any follow-up items (e.g., add monitoring alerts, change cron schedule, increase limits).

Reflection

Which checklist step would you automate first to shorten mean time to detect?

Three compact reminders to carry into your next troubleshooting session.

What to remember
Resource Lanes

fullNarratorScript:
Performance monitoring is the practice of watching C P U, memory, disk input and output and network input and output so you can spot bottlenecks before they affect users. In this chapter we treat these four resources as lanes or pipes: when one lane fills, traffic backs up and the system slows. You will learn practical commands that give real-time and historical views, how to interpret load averages and swap activity, and a repeatable troubleshooting workflow to identify the root cause. We’ll also show how to find and handle runaway processes and how simple limits like ulimit can prevent a single user or process from taking down a server. By the end you’ll be able to collect evidence, choose the right tool, and decide whether to tune, restart, or add capacity. Think of this as a detective process: gather facts, isolate the lane that is saturated, and act on the smallest reliable change that improves response time.

These objectives describe the practical skills you will leave this chapter with. First, you will be able to identify the four primary system resources that cause slowdowns: C P U, memory, disk input and output and network input and output. That means knowing which metric to inspect when a server feels slow. Second, you will learn to operate the common command-line tools used for real-time and historical analysis, such as top, htop, free, vmstat, iostat, mpstat and sar. Third, you will practice diagnosing common performance problems — high C P U usage, memory pressure and slow disks — by collecting evidence and choosing the right follow-up tool. Lastly, you will learn to identify runaway processes and apply basic resource controls, including ulimit and configuration edits to prevent resource exhaustion. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can check your understanding and practice the exact command sequences in a lab.

We continue with four additional, tightly focused objectives you should master. First, become comfortable reading and comparing per-core C P U metrics with mpstat so you can see if one core is overloaded while others idle. Second, practice using free and vmstat to tell the difference between 'free' and 'available' memory, and to spot swap activity that signals memory pressure. Third, learn to interpret iostat: watch %util and await to detect slow disks and when to suspect the storage layer. Fourth, capture historical patterns with sar and use that trend data to avoid assumptions about sporadic slowdowns. Each objective is measurable: run the command, capture output, and explain what it shows. These objectives bridge immediate diagnosis and longer-term capacity planning. Learning Objectives — Continued means per-core metrics, memory available vs free, disk await, and historical sar data are the signals that guide correct remediation choices.. In practical terms, deeper skills and workflow steps to practice. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

C P U monitoring begins with a simple claim: if the C P U lane is saturated, processes wait for execution time and responsiveness drops. The interactive tools top and htop show real-time per-process C P U percent and load averages. Load averages are a compact signal: they show the average number of runnable or uninterruptible processes over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. A useful rule is to compare load averages to the number of C P U cores; a load much higher than core count indicates C P U contention. Use mpstat -P ALL to inspect each core. This detects cases where one core is maxed while others sit idle; that pattern often points to a single-threaded process or improper C P U affinity. A concrete example: run top, observe a process showing 95% C P U on one core while the 1-minute load is near the core count. Run mpstat -P ALL 1 and watch the per-core usage spike on a single C P U. A common misconception is assuming high C P U always means you need more cores; instead first inspect what the offending process is doing and whether it can be optimized or restarted. Key actions: identify the PID in top or htop, inspect its logs or command line, and test terminating a runaway process carefully. Takeaway: collect both per-process and per-core metrics before deciding to add capacity.

Memory pressure is a frequent and subtle cause of slow systems. A key point is that Linux uses spare R A M for cache and buffers, so the raw 'free' column is a poor indicator of health. Instead focus on the 'available' field in free -h; it estimates memory that can be used without swapping. Use vmstat to see short-term trends and swap activity: the si and so columns report swap in and swap out. High values in si/so indicate the kernel is moving pages to or from disk, which is slow and causes latency. A concrete example: run free -h and find available memory under 200MB with swap nearly full; then run vmstat 1 and see repeated non-zero si/so — this is classic memory exhaustion. A common misconception is to immediately add swap; swap can mask the problem but will slow applications. Prefer finding the process that holds large memory, resizing or restarting it, or adding physical R A M when the working set truly exceeds available memory. Practice: use free -h, then vmstat 1 5, and inspect processes in top sorted by memory. Ask yourself which process holds the largest resident set and whether it can be tuned or restarted.

Disk input and output problems often translate directly into slow application response, especially for databases and storage-heavy workloads. The iostat tool reports reads, writes, device utilization and latency. Key metrics are %util, r/s and w/s, kilobytes per second, and await. A high %util near 100 percent means the device was busy and likely a bottleneck. High await indicates long input and output service times. Use iostat -xz 1 to get extended per-device stats. Also check df -h for disk fill levels; a full filesystem can cause surprising failures even if IO rates are modest. A concrete example: run iostat -xz 1 while issuing a large write with dd to simulate load. You will see %util climb and await rise. A common mistake is viewing only throughput without latency; throughput can be high while await is also high, indicating slow response. Practical steps: identify the device (sda, nvme0n1), check %util and await, inspect filesystem usage with df -h, and consider IO scheduler, asynchronous tasks, or moving data to faster storage. Key takeaway: latency matters as much as megabytes per second. Disk I/O Monitoring with iostat and df means watch both %util and await. high utilization with high await points to a slow device, not just heavy throughput.. In practical terms, interpret %util, await, throughput and spot full disks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Network saturation can mimic other bottlenecks. The sar utility with the DEV option reports per-interface rx and tx rates and helps you see trends over time. Use sar -n DEV 1 to sample traffic every second. Key counters include rxkB/s and txkB/s. For real-time per-connection views try iftop or nload to see which flows consume bandwidth. A concrete example: run sar -n DEV 1 and notice rxkB/s rising close to the interface capacity during a backup; iftop will show the IP addresses responsible. A common misconception is to assume all high network rates are problematic — if your link is provisioned for that throughput and latency remains low, high utilization may be normal. Instead look for saturation that causes packet drops or increased latency. Practical steps: identify which interface is busy, check link speed and errors with ethtool, inspect rx/tx rates with sar or iftop, and consider rate-limiting or moving large transfers to off-peak windows. Always correlate network metrics with application response times so you act on real bottlenecks, not expected traffic spikes. Network I/O: sar and real-time tools means use sar for historical interface rates and iftop for per-connection views; correlate traffic with latency and packet errors before acting.. In practical terms, detect saturated interfaces and per-connection bandwidth use. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. When a single process consumes excessive resources it can bring the whole system down. The workflow in the chapter gives a clear sequence: start with top or htop to get a quick system view; identify whether C P U, memory, disk, or network is the likely bottleneck; then drill down with the specialized tool for that resource. For runaway processes, locate the PID and check its command line, open files, and logs. Use kill or restart the service as appropriate; kill -9 should be a last resort because it prevents graceful cleanup. To prevent recurrence, set resource limits with ulimit or via system configuration files such as /etc/security/limits. conf; for example limiting open files per group reduces the risk of descriptor exhaustion. A concrete example: discover multiple bash loops spawned in the background with top, confirm with ps aux | grep bash, then kill the offending PIDs and add a ulimit entry for the user group to cap nofile. Common mistakes include jumping to hardware upgrades before investigating the faulty process and misinterpreting cached memory as free. Close investigations by verifying performance after the change and by collecting historical data with sar to confirm the issue is resolved. Question for reflection: after stopping a runaway process, what evidence will you collect to prevent it from recurring?

Before you can diagnose intermittent performance issues, you need a reproducible way to collect both real-time and historical data. Install the lightweight packages sysstat and htop on your system. htop gives a colored, interactive view of processes and per-core usage for quick triage. sysstat provides the sar, iostat, and mpstat commands that record system activity to disk so you can analyze trends after the fact. On Debian or Ubuntu use the package manager to install and on RHEL derivatives use dnf or yum. After installation, enable or configure the service that records sar data; many distributions require enabling and starting the sysstat service so daily binary logs are written to slash var slash log slash sa. A concrete example: install, enable the service, and verify that slash var slash log slash sa contains files. A common misconception is that sar runs automatically right after package install; often you need to enable collection or adjust cron/systemd timers. Finally, confirm htop launches and sar -V reports a version. This preparation ensures you can gather live snapshots with htop and long-term trends with sar, which together let you spot momentary spikes versus sustained degradation. What small test will you run to confirm data is being recorded?

When diagnosing performance, controlled reproductions are invaluable. You can gently stress C P U and disk to observe how the system responds and which metrics change. For C P U testing, a tight background loop is an easy tool: run an innocuous busy loop in a new shell to raise C P U usage and watch htop and the load averages rise. For disk input and output, a buffered write like the dd command copying from slash dev slash zero to a large file simulates sustained write traffic; monitor iostat -xz 1 to watch %util, r slash s and await change. Always test on non-production systems or use limited counts and smaller file sizes: the common mistake is running an unlimited test that floods production disks or fills capacity. A concrete example is to run one short C P U worker per core and a dd that writes 1 gigabyte — observe htop, iostat and sar simultaneously. Interpret results: high load average with low disk %util points to C P U contention; near 100% device %util and rising await indicate a disk bottleneck. After the test, clean up temporary files and stop background loops. This controlled approach gives clear cause-and-effect between the workload you created and the metrics recorded, and it teaches you how to read the changes in real time and from sar logs later.

Performance issues are often intermittent: they happen at peak hours or during irregular jobs. That's where sar becomes indispensable. sar reads binary data files generated by sysstat and summarizes C P U, memory, input and output, and network activity over time. Start by identifying available sar files in slash var slash log slash sa and use sar -u -f to show historical C P U usage or sar -n DEV -f for network interfaces. Look at the timestamps and compare busy windows to expected workload schedules. A concrete example: if users report slow response at 02:00, open the sar file for that day and run sar -u -f slash var slash log slash sa slash sa21 to inspect C P U averages around that time. Remember to compare sar reports across days to rule out one-off spikes. A common misconception is treating a single high reading as evidence of a persistent problem. Instead, analyze the pattern: isolated spikes require different remediation than sustained high usage. Use sar's per-interval output to correlate events — for example, a cron job that runs hourly may align with disk await increases. Finally, export sar data to CSV if you need to plot trends externally. Historical analysis lets you move from guesswork to evidence-based decisions about tuning or capacity planning.

Preventing a single user or process from exhausting system resources is an important defensive step. ulimit controls shell-level resource limits like the number of open files, maximum memory size, and number of processes. Use ulimit -n to view or set the open file limit for the current shell; changes here are immediate but ephemeral. For persistent, system-wide or user-specific limits, configure slash etc slash security slash limits. conf or drop files into slash etc slash security slash limits. d. For example, to limit members of a webusers group to 1024 open files, add a line that sets hard nofile 1024 for @webusers. A common pitfall is to assume limits. conf applies to services started by systemd. To enforce limits for systemd-managed services, set Limit NOFILE equals or other Limit directives directly in the unit file, because systemd does not always read PAM limits for services. A concrete example: update limits. conf, relogin to a shell, then verify ulimit -n reflects the new limit. Also, test failure modes by creating a process that hits the limit; a graceful failure is preferable to a system-wide crash. In short, ulimit provides immediate control, limits. conf makes those controls persistent for interactive logins, and systemd unit directives are necessary for services started at boot. A consistent workflow turns guesswork into reliable troubleshooting. Start with a snapshot: run top or htop for a high-level view of C P U, memory, and processes. Next, identify which resource shows abnormal signals: high load averages, low available memory, high disk %util, or saturated network interfaces. Then drill down using specialized tools: vmstat for memory and swap activity, iostat for device delays and sar for historical corroboration. Identify the culprit process with ps or by filtering top, and examine its logs and configuration. Decide whether to restart or gracefully stop the service; use kill only when necessary and prefer SIGTERM before SIGKILL. After remediation, monitor to confirm the problem is resolved and that no secondary issues appear. Include these additional checks in your routine: check for full disks with df -h, ensure ulimits are adequate, and review scheduled tasks that might coincide with the spike. A common mistake is assuming that adding C P U or R A M fixes the problem; optimization or configuration changes can be cheaper and faster. Finish by documenting findings and any changes you made so you can spot recurring patterns next time. This disciplined loop — observe, identify, drill down, remediate, and confirm — reduces risk and speeds recovery. Which step in the flow would you automate in your environment?

Let's recap the essential ideas for performance monitoring and troubleshooting. First, C P U, memory, disk input and output, and network input and output are the four resource lanes that can bottleneck a system. Second, use the right tool for the question: htop and top for live triage, vmstat for memory and swap patterns, iostat for device latency and utilization, and sar for historical trends. Third, controlled tests — bounded C P U loops and limited-size dd writes — produce reproducible metrics and help you link actions to symptoms. Fourth, prevent exhaustion with resource limits: use ulimit for quick changes, limits. conf for persistent interactive limits, and Limit directives in systemd unit files for services. Finally, follow a repeatable troubleshooting workflow: snapshot, identify the bottleneck, drill down with focused tools, remediate carefully, and confirm the outcome. Remember these summaries as quick anchors when an alert arrives: observe first, gather evidence, and always verify that your fix resolved the underlying cause.

A few practical reminders before you finish. First, interpret free carefully: focus on the available field rather than raw free, since Linux caches memory for efficiency. Second, %util and await from iostat are your primary disk performance indicators — near 100% utilization and rising await show a disk bottleneck. Third, use sar-collected historical data to catch intermittent problems; do not ignore trends just because a current snapshot looks fine. Fourth, prefer graceful termination of processes and avoid excessive use of kill -9, which prevents cleanup. Lastly, document every investigation: timestamps, commands used, and the action taken so future incidents are faster to resolve. Keep these short rules as part of your operational checklist and you'll reduce unnecessary escalations and misdiagnoses in the future.
